evidence.relevance_note: Directly answers the question: in patients with prior MI or prior stroke/TIA (secondary prevention), aspirin significantly REDUCES recurrent serious vascular events, with a ~19% proportional reduction (rate ratio 0.81, p<0.0001). evidence.text: In the 16 secondary prevention trials (17,000 individuals at high average risk, 43,000 person-years, 3306 serious vascular events), aspirin allocation yielded a greater absolute reduction in serious vascular events (6.7% vs 8.2% per year, p<0.0001), with reductions of about a fifth in total stroke (2.08% vs 2.54% per year, p=0.002) and in coronary events (4.3% vs 5.3% per year, p<0.0001). Rate ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.75-0.87).
evidence.title: Aspirin in the primary and secondary prevention of vascular disease: collaborative meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomised trials

evidence.relevance_note: Independent landmark meta-analysis confirming the same answer: antiplatelet therapy (chiefly aspirin) in patients with established vascular disease reduces recurrent serious vascular events by roughly one quarter, with large absolute benefits in prior-MI and prior-stroke/TIA groups. Corroborates the 2009 Lancet update.
evidence.text: Among high-risk patients with established/acute vascular disease, antiplatelet therapy (mainly aspirin) reduced serious vascular events by about one quarter, non-fatal MI by about one third, non-fatal stroke by about one quarter, and vascular mortality by about one sixth. Absolute reductions per 1000: 36 (SE 5) over 2 years after prior MI; 38 (5) per month in acute MI; 36 (6) over 2 years after prior stroke/TIA. Low-dose (75-150 mg) aspirin was as effective as higher doses.
evidence.title: Collaborative meta-analysis of randomised trials of antiplatelet therapy for prevention of death, myocardial infarction, and stroke in high risk patients

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: confident YES with the key figures (RR 0.81, 6.7% vs 8.2%/yr, ~19-25% reduction) cited to both packet sources.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. Aspirin reduces recurrent serious vascular events in patients with established cardiovascular disease. The Antithrombotic Trialists' Collaboration 2009 Lancet meta-analysis of 16 secondary-prevention trials (17,000 patients, 43,000 person-years, 3306 events) found aspirin lowered serious vascular events from 8.2% to 6.7% per year, a rate ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.75-0.87; p<0.0001) and an ~19% proportional reduction, with about a fifth reductions in both total stroke (2.08% vs 2.54%/yr) and coronary events (4.3% vs 5.3%/yr). The earlier 2002 ATT BMJ meta-analysis independently found antiplatelet therapy (mainly aspirin) reduced serious vascular events by about one quarter in high-risk patients with established disease, with roughly 36 fewer events per 1000 over two years after prior MI or prior stroke/TIA. The benefit is decisive and consistent across both meta-analyses.

The provided trials are observational summaries that pool heterogeneous populations with prior MI, stroke, and TIA, and the absolute differences (6.7% vs 8.2% per year) are modest and could be confounded by differences in baseline risk and concomitant therapy. Without patient-level randomisation details, dose standardisation, and bleeding trade-off data for each individual trial, the evidence here is too uncertain to conclude that aspirin actually reduces recurrent serious vascular events. A firm conclusion would require additional trials and data not contained in this packet.

ground_truth.answer: YES. Aspirin reduces recurrent serious vascular events in patients with established cardiovascular disease (secondary prevention). The Antithrombotic Trialists' (ATT) Collaboration 2009 Lancet meta-analysis of 16 secondary-prevention trials (17,000 patients) found aspirin reduced serious vascular events from 8.2% to 6.7% per year (rate ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.75-0.87; p<0.0001), an ~19% proportional reduction, with about a fifth reduction in both total stroke and coronary events. The earlier 2002 ATT BMJ meta-analysis similarly found antiplatelet therapy (mainly aspirin) cut serious vascular events by about one quarter in high-risk patients with established disease (e.g., ~36 fewer events per 1000 over 2 years after prior MI or prior stroke/TIA).
ground_truth.why_answerable: Both packet documents are large, individual-participant-data and trial-level meta-analyses that directly report statistically significant, clinically large reductions in recurrent serious vascular events with aspirin in secondary-prevention populations, with consistent figures and tight confidence intervals (p<0.0001). The evidence is sufficient and decisive for a confident YES.
